title: Why even release your slop?
author: ckau
selftext:
I don't wanna play your game. I will not buy your game. My Claude have built five games for me yesterday already, tailored to my tastes and following my grand ~~theftauto~~ design ideas. 

Besides, I have hundreds of games on Steam in my *backlog*, already.

If there's a tool that allows **anyone** to build **anything**, and there's no limitation to it, no craftsmanship required... then, there's no need for a market. There's no need for releases. 

Indie gamedev is a TikTok now - your game might start a trend. But no one will buy it, everyone will just make a copy of it. Your game will not go viral, it will become a trend for a week or so. You will get nothing out of it.

It's the same with anything AI - AI music, AI art, AI ads... I call it slop when I hear/see it, because I was not the one who made it, simple as that. I don't wanna to hear your Suno music in my Spotify, simply because I already have my own Suno subscription, and it ***IS*** my "Spotify".

Pygmalion effect of loving own creation is strong with AI artists and developers. And so the most things considered "art" or "interactive art" are only attractive to those who create it. "Publishing" it is a nonsense, just another drop into dead internet theory. 

I'm totally okay with this. The more we accelerate heat death of internet and culture, the faster we will come to this point of self-sufficient masturbation of own ego and cravings for art, the sooner we will fall out of this and either come back to craftsmanship again, or make a leap into post-human era, sorta Matrix thing, where each individual is truly living in an isolated shell that knows what he or she wants even before he or she knows it. Perfect personal heaven... what will be the cost is an open question.

Anyhow - Why even release your slop?

comments.body: So even though anyone can use the tools not everyone is willing to put in the thousands of hours or the months or potentially years worth of credits to make a good ai assisted game. There are a lot of slop games but there are also some high effort ai good assisted games. I’ve found a middle ground with high effort slop personally

comments.author: AMSolar
comments.body:
Fixing small things around the house is something that anyone can do, but handymans still have a job and make good living.

Same here. Most people don't even know you could install codex on your computer and ask it to generate games. Or even if they do know their first 5-10 prompts generates total garbage and they give up and never try it again.

That's why people will play these games. They might become dramatically cheaper or shift towards free model like smartphone game slop.  
By the way smartphone games were NEVER not slop, they were slop even before AI.

Now the PC and console games just follow the same direction and it'll be fine.   
  
Most stuff will never see the light of day, but most stuff didn't see the light of day before AI either.

comments.author: Negative_Leave5161
comments.body: People are buying my stuff just fine.

comments.author: Zimgar
comments.body:
For a couple reasons -

1. People often don't realize their creations are 'slop'.  This has always been the case even before AI, you can find hundreds and thousands of terrible games or products out there.  AI has just made it easier to create.  
2. The hope for money or random success.  People buy into the theory that they can make it big, some games get viral, and many times people don't really understand why a game might become viral.  Often those that create slop can't recognize the difference between good games and slop themselves.

comments.author: Odd_Revolution7522
comments.body:
I think you are actually right, but for a way narrower use case than you probably think.

You can make five games in a day with Claude, but *what kind of game* ? If you want a game with very simple mechanics but custom theme or art, then yes your approach basically works.

Flappy Bird in space, Hotline Miami in a different setting with different enemies and weapons, sure, fine. And even that latter example would probably take at least a weekend if you want to make it really fun.

But you also suffer from a misunderstanding of what AI is and its current capabilities. I have been working on my game for three months. Yes Astra, Sol, Fable or Opus are fast and quite capable. But a complex systemic game, well balanced and with coherent art direction still requires a ton of work.

A few blind spots I think you have :

\- AAA games are still way beyond what a solo amateur vibecoder can do.

\- Many people just want to play games instead of spending time creating them.

\- One of the main pleasures of playing games is to discover new ideas and experiences made by people who have a different mindset and ideas. If you specify yourself the game you want, then you mostly destroy the element of surprise.

comments.author: SlightOfHand_
comments.body: Why be a dungeon master when you can simply write a fantasy novel and never show it to anyone

comments.author: sunsparkswift
comments.body:
I enjoyed what I made. If someone else might enjoy it, why not at least put it out there? Perhaps it'll only appeal to me. But perhaps it'll also appeal to some others like me who don't want to spend the time making it, because it still takes time and effort, if not nearly as much so as before AI. And perhaps someone will be inspired by it to do their own thing? Someone posted a GBA game they made here at one point, and that greatly inspired me to do a "small scope spin off project" that ended up being something I'm glad I spent my time on.  
Star Trek is one of the things I grew up with and I think in the end, it'll end up a bit like the holodeck. Some people made programs for themselves, but others wanted something that appealed to them but didn't come directly from their own head so they could be surprised and have a sense of discovery, so even though it was as easy as prompting a computer, holodeck creations by others were still released and spread.
